COLLEGE NEWS

MILITARY NEWS
USS VERMONT SSN 792
On Oct. 29, the USS VERMONT (SSN 792) arrived at HMAS Stirling, the Royal Australian Navy’s largest naval base, to begin the most extensive Submarine Maintenance Period ever performed outside of U.S. territory.
This event is a step within the AUKUS Tri-Lateral pact between Australia, the U.K. and the U.S. and precursor to the start of regular deployments of Virginia Class nuclear submarines to Western Australia in 2027. They will become a component of the Submarine Rotational Force-West Pacific.
The submarine, nicknamed “Big Sugar” in a nod to Vermont’s famous flavor, arrived at HMAS Stirling with a predominantly American crew that also included Royal Australian Navy and U.K. Royal Navy submariners.
AROUND TOWN
Veterans Day
NORTHFIELD — Norwich University and Northfield will combine to host a series of events honoring service and community.
Friday, Nov. 7: Veterans Day Ceremony, 4:15 to 5 p.m., Norwich University Upper Parade Ground, rain or shine; sixth annual Darn Tough Sock Toss Game community outreach benefit, 7 p.m., Kreitzberg Arena.
Monday, Nov. 10: U.S. Marine Corps Cake-Cutting Ceremony 250th birthday commemoration, 11 a.m., Kreitzberg Library; Lunch & Learn Conversation discussion focused on a life of service, noon, Todd Multipurpose Room, Kreitzberg Library.
Tuesday, Nov. 11: Northfield Veterans Day observance hosted by American Legion Post 63, 11 a.m., Northfield Town Common.
Immigration films
BARRE — In partnership with Migrant Justice, film historian Rick Winston will present “The Other Side of Hope: Films about Immigration” from 7 to 8:30 p.m. Wednesday, Nov. 12, at Socialist Labor Party Hall, 46 Granite St., Barre. Suggested donation $10. For more information, email info@oldlaborhall.org or call 802-505-0405.
AROUND VT
Smoke alarms
The American Red Cross encourages everyone to test their smoke alarms when daylight savings time ends as they turn their clocks back, to make sure the devices are working.
Install smoke alarms on every level of your home, including inside and outside bedrooms and sleeping areas.
Replace smoke alarms that are 10 years or older. Components such as sensors can become less sensitive over time. Follow your alarm’s manufacturer instructions.
Practice your two-minute home fire escape plan. Make sure everyone in your household can get out in less than two minutes — the amount of time you may have to escape a burning home before it’s too late.
Include at least two ways to get out of every room and select a meeting spot at a safe distance away from your home, such as your neighbor’s home or landmark like a specific tree in your front yard, where everyone can meet.
Visit redcross.org/fire for more information, including an escape plan to create and practice with your family, or download the free Red Cross Emergency app by searching “American Red Cross” in app stores.
If you cannot afford to purchase smoke alarms or are physically unable to install one, the Red Cross may be able to help. Vermont residents can visit redcross.org/EndHomesFiresNNE or call 1-800-464-6692 (Option 4) to schedule a free installation. A member of the Red Cross team will follow up to schedule your smoke alarm appointment.
Evening commute
With the end of Daylight Saving Time bringing earlier sunsets, the Vermont Highway Safety Alliance is reminding drivers to be extra cautious during the evening commute. The earlier onset of darkness increases the risk of vehicle crashes due to reduced visibility and driver fatigue.
The combination of reduced light and changes in sleep patterns can create hazardous driving conditions for motorists, pedestrians and cyclists alike. To stay safe:
— Slow down, especially during dawn and dusk when visibility is lowest.
— Leave extra space between your vehicle and the one ahead.
— Keep headlights on to improve visibility and ensure all vehicle lights are functioning properly.
— Clean your car windows and headlights to maximize visibility and be vigilant not to drive distracted.
— Stay alert for pedestrians and cyclists, particularly in neighborhoods and at crosswalks.
Get vaccinated
With winter approaching, Vermont health officials are encouraging everyone to take steps to protect themselves, their families and their communities from flu, COVID-19 and RSV, including getting vaccinated.
This season’s flu and COVID-19 vaccines are updated to target the most recent strains of the viruses and are recommended for everyone age 6 months and older. Immunizations for RSV are also widely available for pregnant people, infants and older adults.
People at higher risk of serious illness, including older adults, infants and young children, pregnant people, and those with weakened immune systems, are especially encouraged to get vaccinated.
Vermont health officials published updated recommendations for the COVID-19 vaccine this year to help ensure anyone who wants the vaccine is able to get it. Anyone age 5 and up can get COVID-19 and flu vaccines at a pharmacy. Vaccines are also available through health care providers, including for children under age 5.
Health insurance will cover the cost for most people to get vaccinated. Adults younger than 65 without health insurance, or whose insurance does not include immunizations, can get vaccines at no cost through their local health office.
Like any medicine, vaccines can cause side effects. They’re usually mild, like a sore arm or feeling tired for a day or two.
Italian culture grant
The Vermont Italian Cultural Association announced its grant program to encourage exploration of Italy’s culture, is once again accepting applications now.
The program provides up to $1,500 in funding to three individuals seeking to learn more about the Italian American experience, Italian language, arts, music, food, history, or any aspect of Italian culture.
Individuals interested in applying will find an application in the grants section, under Programs, on the VICA website at vermontitalianculturalassociation.org. Applications are being accepted through March 1.
VTF&W
Wildlife sightings
Vermont Fish & Wildlife Department is asking hunters to participate in its annual deer hunter effort and sighting survey. The survey asks hunters to record how many hours they hunted and how many deer, moose, bears or other wildlife they saw each day they hunted.
To complete the survey, use the Deer Hunting Log feature in the Vermont Outdoors mobile app available through the App Store or Google Play. A web-based version of the survey will also be available on Fish & Wildlife’s website after the start of the regular season on Nov. 15.
Deer teeth
Vermont Fish & Wildlife Department is asking hunters for help gathering biological data on the state’s deer population. Hunters who get a deer during the Nov. 15-30 regular deer season are asked to provide an incisor tooth from their deer. Tooth envelopes are available at all deer reporting stations.
Biologists are collecting middle incisor teeth from all regular season bucks to evaluate regional differences in ages and antler characteristics, as well as to help estimate population size, growth rate, health, and mortality rates.
